newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Europe should heed Albania cry for help - Vranitzky.
newsitem.headline: Europe should heed Albania cry for help - Vranitzky.

text.p: OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky has said there is no alternative to foreign intervention to stem the wave of anarchy in Albania and has stressed the urgency of his appeal in talks with European and U.S. leaders.

"The Albanian government has cried out for outside support in the form of military and police force participation. As they are a member of Europe we can not ignore this plea," Vranitzky told reporters on his return to Vienna on Friday after talks with Albanian government and rebel leaders.

The former Austrian chancellor, leading a mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), held talks with Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Foreign Minister Arjan Starova and army chief of staff General Adem Copani on the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic.
He later met 15 representatives of rebel towns in the south, where an insurgency broke out two weeks ago after protests over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
"I will report that there is no alternative (to foreign intervention) as far as I can see," Vranitzky told reporters.

"A coalition of willing (participants) should be created so that decisions can be made swiftly," he said, stressing that a request for outside military help should be made to individual governments rather than to any particular body.

Vranitzky said he had already briefed several foreign ministers on the talks by telephone, including U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos.

He said he had also spoken to Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the presidency of the European Union and Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current OSCE chairman.

Vranitzky acknowledged that support from OSCE members was unlikely to be unanimous but dismissed the assertion by Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok that any intervention would require United Nations approval.
"We have been invited in by the Albanian government. It is now up to individual countries to decide whether they want to send in their people," Vranitzky said.
The OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council was due to meet in special session on Saturday to discuss Vranitzky's report.

The Albanian government told the OSCE delegation it wanted a foreign police force of around 4,000. But that number appeared unlikely to be anywhere near the presence needed to halt anarchy throughout the Balkan state.

"We are now in a situation where the government, President (Sali) Berisha, political parties and rebel committees want the same goal. To restore public order, to restore democracy and to have new elections," Vranitzky said earlier at a news conference in the Italian port Brindisi.
"In Albania there is not a civil war, there is unrest, uproar against the political solution which so many Albanians believe to be unjust," Vranitzky added.
Rebels in the south have turned their outrage on Berisha, insisting that he should step down before they help to restore order.
Despite some concessions by Berisha -- the head of his feared Shik secret police resigned on Friday -- he has given no sign he is prepared to step down.
Vranitzky said members of the National Committee of Public Salvation -- the umbrella group of rebel towns -- blamed Berisha for the current unrest.
"They said it was all Berisha's fault, so he shouldn't grace his office any more," Vranitzky said.
